Worked example: five designs, from a treatment effect to an instrument

Source: vignettes/articles/worked-example.Rmd
worked-example.Rmd

This page takes five study designs through powerape, each in R and in Stata. The teams are stylized; the questions are the ones a design discussion has to answer:

  • Design A. How many observations does a treatment effect worth acting on need?
  • Design B. Can a moderation study find its interaction?
  • Design C. What is last year’s pilot worth for next year’s design?
  • Design D. How many firms does a firm-year panel need?
  • Design E. What does instrumenting the treatment cost?

Each section states the setting, runs the calls that answer the question and draws the lesson. The lessons are collected at the end, with what a power analysis of this kind should report. Choosing R or Stata on any tab switches the whole page.

The R code fixes its seeds, so its numbers reproduce exactly with the version of the package named at the end. Stata draws different random numbers, so its numbers agree with R’s up to simulation error; the text quotes the two side by side. In Stata, a single power call fits every simulated study with Stata’s own estimation command (probit, or cfprobit in Design E), and the searches and sweeps use the faster Mata engine (see Get started in Stata).

Claims, in one paragraph

Every design is priced for a claim about the confidence interval of the effect, stated in probability points (Riesthuis, 2024). The minimum-effect claim (minimum, the default) holds when the lower bound of the interval exceeds the smallest effect size of interest (the SESOI), so the effect is large enough to matter; detection (detect) holds when the interval excludes zero; equivalence holds when the interval lies within ±SESOI. Designs A, C and D are priced for the minimum-effect claim, B and E for detection. Power is the share of simulated studies in which the claim holds, and a required sample size is found by search and then confirmed by a run four times as long.

Design A: a treatment effect worth acting on

A team plans an archival study of a support program for firms. Without the program, about 30 percent of firms survive the study window. Firm characteristics explain a modest share of the latent variation in survival; one standard-normal covariate with a signal of 0.10 stands in for them. The program pays for itself if it raises survival by five percentage points, and earlier evidence puts its effect near ten. The study should be able to conclude that the program is worth its cost: a minimum-effect claim with a SESOI of 0.05. This is the design question of the home page, with the same seeds, taken all the way through here.

library(powerape)

dA <- ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
              covariates = list(pa_var("z", "normal")),
              baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10)
dA <- set_ape(dA, target = 0.10)
dA
#> powerape DGP -- probit
#>   focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
#>   covariates: z (normal, mean 0.00, sd 1.00) 
#>   baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.100
#>   true APE pinned at +0.1000 (beta_focal = 0.2857, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.400)
powerape dgp a, focal(program, binary p(0.5)) covariates((z, normal))      ///
    baseline(0.30) signal(0.10)
powerape setape a, target(0.10)
powerape DGP -- probit
  focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
  covariates: z (normal, mean 0.00, sd 1.00)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.100
  target effect not set yet - run powerape setape or powerape setaie.

powerape DGP -- probit
  focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
  covariates: z (normal, mean 0.00, sd 1.00)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.100
  true APE pinned at + 0.1000 (beta_focal =    0.2857, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.400)

Power at 1,500 firms 

pA <- ape_power(dA, n = 1500, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                nsim = 4000, seed = 501)
pA
#> powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
#>   probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE +0.1000, 90% CI (alpha = 0.05), nsim = 4000
#>   power = 0.663 (MCSE 0.007)
#>   outcomes: minimum 0.663 | detect-only 0.323 | inconclusive 0.014 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000
powerape power a, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(4000) seed(501)
powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 4000
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)
  power = 0.677 (MCSE 0.007)
  outcomes: minimum 0.677 | detect-only 0.312 | inconclusive 0.011 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

At 1,500 firms the minimum-effect claim holds in 66 percent of the simulated studies (Stata: 68). The outcome table shows where the others end: in 32 percent the interval excludes zero but not 0.05. Those studies would find that the program works and still could not say that it is worth its cost.

The required sample size 

nA_min <- ape_n(dA, power = 0.80, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                nsim = 1000, seed = 502)
nA_det <- ape_n(dA, power = 0.80, claim = "detect", nsim = 1000, seed = 503)
nA_min
#> powerape required sample size -- minimum claim
#>   n = 2091 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.808, MCSE 0.006)
#>   assumed true APE +0.1000, sesoi 0.050, 90% CI (alpha = 0.05), probit
#>   search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.
nA_det
#> powerape required sample size -- detect claim
#>   n = 663 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.803, MCSE 0.006)
#>   assumed true APE +0.1000, sesoi -, 95% CI (alpha = 0.05), probit
#>   search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.
powerape n a, power(0.80) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(1000) seed(502)  ///
    engine(mata)
local n_min = r(n)

powerape n a, power(0.80) claim(detect) nsim(1000) seed(503) engine(mata)
powerape required sample size -- minimum claim
  n = 2084 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.800, MCSE 0.006)
  assumed true APE + 0.1000, sesoi 0.050,     90% CI (alpha =    .05), probit
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.

powerape required sample size -- detect claim
  n = 663 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.796, MCSE 0.006)
  assumed true APE + 0.1000, sesoi -,     95% CI (alpha =    .05), probit
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.

For 80 percent power the minimum-effect claim needs 2,091 firms and detection 663 (Stata: 2,084 and 663; the Stata code keeps its required n in a local for the steps that follow). Concluding that the effect matters costs 3.2 times the sample of concluding that it exists, so a study sized for detection would be about a third of the size its authors need for the conclusion they want to draw.

How much the guesses matter

The baseline rate and the signal are informed guesses. A sweep re-prices the design at the required n over baselines from 0.20 to 0.40 and signals from 0 to 0.30.

rA <- ape_robust(dA, n = nA_min$n, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                 vary = list(baseline = c(0.20, 0.40), signal = c(0, 0.30)),
                 grid_points = 3, nsim = 600, seed = 504, nmax = FALSE)
rA
#> powerape robustness sweep -- minimum claim, APE, pin = ape
#>   n = 2091, nsim = 600 per scenario, 9 scenario(s) over: baseline, signal
#>   power range [0.755, 0.902]; worst scenario:
#>  baseline signal implied_effect power       mcse separated
#>       0.4      0            0.1 0.755 0.01755824         0
#>   scenarios:
#>  baseline signal implied_effect     power       mcse separated
#>       0.2   0.00            0.1 0.8316667 0.01527510         0
#>       0.3   0.00            0.1 0.7733333 0.01709234         0
#>       0.4   0.00            0.1 0.7550000 0.01755824         0
#>       0.2   0.15            0.1 0.8766667 0.01342400         0
#>       0.3   0.15            0.1 0.7633333 0.01735202         0
#>       0.4   0.15            0.1 0.8250000 0.01551209         0
#>       0.2   0.30            0.1 0.9016667 0.01215620         0
#>       0.3   0.30            0.1 0.8500000 0.01457738         0
#>       0.4   0.30            0.1 0.8066667 0.01612222         0
powerape robust a, n(`n_min') claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05)                   ///
    vary(baseline(0.20 0.40) signal(0 0.30)) gridpoints(3)                 ///
    nsim(600) seed(504) nonmax engine(mata)
powerape robustness sweep -- minimum claim, APE, pin = ape
  n = 2084, nsim = 600 per scenario, 9 scenario(s) over: baseline, signal
  power range [0.732, 0.915]; worst scenario: row 3
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
 row     baseline       signal    implied_eff    power     mcse separated
   1           .2            0         0.1000   0.8350   0.0152    0.0000
   2           .3            0         0.1000   0.7983   0.0164    0.0000
   3           .4            0         0.1000   0.7317   0.0181    0.0000

Across the nine scenarios, power at 2,091 firms runs from 76 to 90 percent (Stata, at its own 2,084: 73 to 92). The weakest scenario combines a baseline of 0.40 with a signal of 0.00, and even there about three studies in four reach the conclusion. The design does not hinge on getting the baseline or the signal exactly right.

Design B: a moderation study that could find its interaction

A second team expects the program to work better for family firms. That is a claim about an interaction, and the effect size that states it is the average interaction effect (AIE): the difference, in probability points, between the program’s effect among family firms and its effect among the others. The team states four numbers on the probability scale: survival of 0.30 for non-family firms without the program, a program effect of ten points among them, a difference of three points between family and other firms without the program, and an interaction of eight points. set_aie() (in Stata, powerape setaie) turns them into a probit whose four cells survive at 0.30, 0.40, 0.33 and 0.51. The design has no covariates. A second world prices the same eight points as a plain main effect of the program.

dB <- set_ape(ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
                      baseline = 0.30), target = 0.08)

dBi <- ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
               moderator = pa_var("family", "binary", p = 0.5),
               baseline = 0.30)
dBi <- set_aie(dBi, target = 0.08, main_focal = 0.10, main_moderator = 0.03)
dBi
#> powerape DGP -- probit
#>   focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
#>   moderator: family (binary, p = 0.50) (focal-by-moderator interaction included)
#>   covariates: none
#>   baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.000
#>   true AIE pinned at +0.0800 (beta_int = 0.1939)
#>   main APEs at reference: program +0.100 (beta = 0.2711), family +0.030 (beta = 0.0845)
powerape dgp b, focal(program, binary p(0.5)) baseline(0.30)
powerape setape b, target(0.08)

powerape dgp bi, focal(program, binary p(0.5))                             ///
    moderator(family, binary p(0.5)) baseline(0.30)
powerape setaie bi, target(0.08) mainfocal(0.10) mainmoderator(0.03)
powerape DGP -- probit
  focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
  moderator: family (binary, p = 0.50) (focal-by-moderator interaction included)
  covariates: none
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.000
  target effect not set yet - run powerape setape or powerape setaie.

powerape DGP -- probit
  focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
  moderator: family (binary, p = 0.50) (focal-by-moderator interaction included)
  covariates: none
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.000
  true AIE pinned at + 0.0800 (beta_int =    0.1939)
  main APEs at reference: program  0.100 (beta =    0.2711), family  0.030 (beta =    0.0845)
nB  <- ape_n(dB,  power = 0.80, claim = "detect", nsim = 1000, seed = 521)
nBi <- ape_n(dBi, power = 0.80, claim = "detect", nsim = 1000, seed = 522)
nB
#> powerape required sample size -- detect claim
#>   n = 1092 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.798, MCSE 0.006)
#>   assumed true APE +0.0800, sesoi -, 95% CI (alpha = 0.05), probit
#>   search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.
nBi
#> powerape required sample size -- detect claim
#>   n = 4514 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.796, MCSE 0.006)
#>   assumed true AIE +0.0800, sesoi -, 95% CI (alpha = 0.05), probit
#>   search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.
powerape n b, power(0.80) claim(detect) nsim(1000) seed(521) engine(mata)

powerape n bi, power(0.80) claim(detect) nsim(1000) seed(522) engine(mata)
powerape required sample size -- detect claim
  n = 1093 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.797, MCSE 0.006)
  assumed true APE + 0.0800, sesoi -,     95% CI (alpha =    .05), probit
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.

  n = 4518 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.793, MCSE 0.006)

Detecting the eight-point interaction with 80 percent power takes 4,514 firms; the same eight points as a main effect take 1,092 (Stata: 4,518 and 1,093). The interaction costs 4.1 times as much. The reason lies in the estimand: the AIE is a difference of differences of four cell rates, each estimated from about a quarter of the sample. Demanding a meaningful interaction, a minimum-effect claim with a SESOI of its own, raises the requirement again (see Interaction effects).

The null side has a claim of its own. An equivalence claim lets a team show that the program’s effect differs between the two kinds of firm by less than a margin it can defend, instead of reading a non-significant interaction test as evidence that the effect is the same everywhere (see Equivalence).

Design C: from last year’s pilot to next year’s design

A third team has a pilot of 900 firms from an earlier wave. The pilot-model route builds the next study’s world from a probit fitted to the pilot: it resamples the pilot’s covariate rows and keeps the fitted nuisance coefficients, but not the program’s coefficient. That one is solved again at the design target, because the pilot’s noisy estimate of the very effect under study is the one thing a design should not inherit. The team targets an effect of eight points and wants to show that it exceeds three.

The pilot is simulated here, so that the page runs anywhere. Stata cannot draw R’s random numbers, so the Stata tab reads the same 900 rows from a file, design-c-pilot.csv, and its probit reproduces R’s coefficients.

set.seed(31)
z        <- rnorm(900)
program  <- rbinom(900, 1, 0.5)
survived <- rbinom(900, 1, pnorm(-0.55 + 0.35 * program + 0.45 * z))
pilot    <- data.frame(survived, program, z)

fit <- glm(survived ~ program + z, family = binomial("probit"), data = pilot)
coef(summary(fit))
#>               Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.5771775 0.06528506 -8.840882 9.496624e-19
#> program      0.3392172 0.08947999  3.790984 1.500515e-04
#> z            0.4577795 0.04796170  9.544688 1.365184e-21
import delimited using "design-c-pilot.csv", asdouble encoding(utf-8) clear
probit survived program z, nolog

dC   <- set_ape(ape_dgp_from_fit(fit, focal = "program"), target = 0.08)
dC25 <- set_ape(ape_dgp_from_fit(fit, focal = "program", baseline = 0.25),
                target = 0.08)
dC

The pilot implies a baseline of 0.303, and at that baseline the design needs 1,986 firms (Stata: 1,985). If the next study will run in a harsher environment, with a baseline of 0.25 instead, one changed argument re-prices the whole design: 1,819 firms (Stata: 1,822). Outcomes near a rate of 0.25 are slightly less noisy than near 0.30, so the same eight points are a little easier to establish.

Two cautions. This is prospective design for the next study, not “observed power” for the pilot, which remains a fallacy (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001). And a world built from a pilot inherits the pilot’s sampling noise: with fewer than 500 pilot rows, powerape warns that the design’s context is itself an estimate.

Design D: a firm-year panel, priced in firms

A fourth team plans a panel: firms observed over four annual waves, an adoption event that is constant within the window, and the outcome, baseline and covariate signal of Design A. The analysis will be a correlated random effects (CRE) probit with Mundlak (1978) means and firm-clustered standard errors, so the design is simulated for that estimator. Two panel quantities must be stated: rho, the share of the unexplained latent variation that is stable within firms (0.30, the rho of xtprobit), and the share of that stable part that tracks the firms’ observed averages (one half). Sample sizes now count firms. The Panel designs workflow describes the route in detail.

dD <- ape_dgp_panel(focal = pa_var("adopt", "binary", p = 0.5, icc = 1),
                    covariates = list(pa_var("size", "normal", icc = 0.6)),
                    n_periods = 4, rho = 0.30, cre_share = 0.50,
                    baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10)
dD <- set_ape(dD, target = 0.10)
dD
#> powerape DGP -- probit
#>   focal: adopt (binary, p = 0.50, icc = 1.00)
#>   covariates: size (normal, mean 0.00, sd 1.00, icc = 0.60) 
#>   panel: 4 periods per unit; rho = 0.30 (latent unit share), cre_share = 0.50; CRE probit w/ Mundlak means, unit-clustered SEs
#>   baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.100
#>   true APE pinned at +0.1000 (beta_focal = 0.3634, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.400)
powerape dgp d, panel focal(adopt, binary p(0.5) icc(1))                   ///
    covariates((size, normal icc(0.6))) nperiods(4) rho(0.30)              ///
    creshare(0.50) baseline(0.30) signal(0.10)
powerape setape d, target(0.10)

  covariates: size (normal, mean 0.00, sd 1.00, icc = 0.60)
  panel: 4 periods per unit; rho = 0.30 (latent unit share), cre_share = 0.50; CRE probit w/
    Mundlak means, unit-clustered SEs
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.100
  target effect not set yet - run powerape setape or powerape setaie.

Panel rows are not independent firms

Three hundred firms over four waves are 1,200 firm-years. The second world draws the same 1,200 rows as independent firms.

pD <- ape_power(dD, n = 300, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                nsim = 20000, seed = 501)
pD
#> powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
#>   probit, n = 300 units x 4 periods (1200 obs), assumed true APE +0.1000, 90% CI (alpha = 0.05), nsim = 20000
#>   power = 0.563 (MCSE 0.004)
#>   outcomes: minimum 0.563 | detect-only 0.388 | inconclusive 0.050 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000
dCS <- set_ape(ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("adopt", "binary", p = 0.5),
                       covariates = list(pa_var("size", "normal")),

The panel of 300 firms reaches 56 percent power for the minimum-effect claim, the 1,200 independent firms 59 percent, 3 points more (Stata: 55 and 58 percent, from 4,000 replications each; R uses 20,000 to pin down a gap this small, but under probit each simulated panel costs Stata many times what it costs R’s engine). Two common intuitions both fail here. Panel rows are not independent firms: when firms differ in unobserved ways, a firm’s repeated rows carry less information than as many new firms would. Nor are they nearly redundant, as the design effects of cluster-randomized trials would suggest: in this world half of the stable firm effect tracks the firms’ observed averages, and the Mundlak means absorb that part instead of wasting it. Even with no firm heterogeneity at all, the CRE estimator would trail a cross-section of the same size, because holding the firm means fixed spends about 1/T of the identifying variation: a premium worth paying, since rho is never known to be zero.

Required firms, and what rho does

Eighty percent power takes 572 firms, or 2,288 firm-years (Stata: 573 firms). As rho moves from 0.10 to 0.50, power at 300 firms falls from 59 to 52 percent (Stata: 59 to 51). Rho, not the number of rows, is the quantity a reviewer should probe: once it is non-trivial, firms rather than rows buy power, and what a panel’s waves are worth is a property of the design that the simulation computes.

Attrition

Firms drop out. The next two worlds keep each firm from one wave to the next with probability 0.85 or 0.70, and the estimator becomes the CRE probit for unbalanced panels of Wooldridge (2019): Mundlak means over the waves a firm is observed, and indicators for the number of those waves.

retained <- function(r) {
  d <- ape_dgp_panel(focal = pa_var("adopt", "binary", p = 0.5, icc = 1),
                     covariates = list(pa_var("size", "normal", icc = 0.6)),
                     n_periods = 4, retention = r, rho = 0.30,
                     cre_share = 0.50, baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10,
                     n_int = 4e4)
  set_ape(d, target = 0.10)
}
dD85 <- retained(0.85)
dD70 <- retained(0.70)
p85 <- ape_power(dD85, n = 300, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,

p70 <- ape_power(dD70, n = 300, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                 nsim = 10000, seed = 71)

             nsim = 800, seed = 72)

             nsim = 800, seed = 72)

Retention of 0.85 and 0.70 leaves 3.2 and 2.5 waves per firm on average. Power at 300 firms falls from 56 to 50 and 44 percent, and the requirement rises from 572 to 699 and 843 firms (Stata: 49 and 42 percent from 2,000 replications each; 701 and 849 firms). In firm-years the three requirements are close, about 2,290, 2,230 and 2,140: what attrition removes is rows per firm, and recruitment has to make them up. A proposal can budget for its expected retention instead of hoping for it.

Design E: what instrumenting a treatment costs

A fifth team studies a treatment that firms choose for themselves, participation in a training program, with a subsidy offer as the instrument. The analysis will be a control-function probit (Wooldridge, 2015): a first-stage probit of participation on the instrument, whose generalized residual enters the outcome probit. This is the estimator of Stata’s cfprobit, and in the Stata tab cfprobit fits every simulated study of a single power call. Two quantities are new: the correlation between the errors of the two equations, which is why the treatment must be instrumented at all (endogeneity, here 0.4), and the strength of the first stage, the instrument’s share of the latent variation in participation (iv_strength, here 0.2). A second world is the same design with an exogenous treatment. The IV designs workflow describes the route in detail.

dE <- ape_dgp_iv(focal = pa_var("training", "binary", p = 0.4),
                 covariates = list(pa_var("size", "normal")),
                 instruments = pa_var("subsidy", "binary", p = 0.5),
                 endogeneity = 0.4, iv_strength = 0.2,
                 baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10)
dE <- set_ape(dE, target = 0.10)

dEx <- set_ape(ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("training", "binary", p = 0.4),
                       covariates = list(pa_var("size", "normal")),
                       baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10), target = 0.10)
dE

At 1,200 observations the exogenous design detects the ten-point APE with 96 percent power, the instrumented design with 22 percent (Stata: 96 and 22). Nothing about the effect changed, only the share of the variation the estimator is allowed to use. The control function identifies the effect mainly from the instrumented share, so its standard error exceeds the exogenous one by roughly the square root of 1/iv_strength, about 2.2 here, and the endogeneity assumed in this world pushes the surcharge higher still.

Detection with 80 percent power takes 699 observations when the treatment is exogenous and 6,813 under the control function (Stata: 732 and 6,750), a factor of 9.7. At this scale power rises slowly with n, so a few hundred observations either way sit within simulation error of 80 percent: the instrumented search uses 2,000 replications per step and confirms its answer with 16,000.

Holding the effect fixed, power at 1,200 observations runs from 12 to 32 percent as the instrument’s share moves from 0.10 to 0.30 (Stata: 14 to 32): first-stage strength is the elicitation that matters most. A moderated version in the spirit of Design B, a six-point AIE between public and private firms with an instrument share of 0.25, reaches only 10 percent power at 2,000 observations (Stata: 10), because it pays both surcharges at once. A study sized for a plain probit that turns to instruments at review time has not gained a robustness check; it has lost the study. Budget for the estimator the analysis will report: a few minutes of simulation show the cost before the data are collected.

The five designs at a glance

Design Question Required n, R Required n, Stata Lesson
A How many firms for an effect worth acting on? 2,091 vs. 663 2,084 vs. 663 A meaningful conclusion costs about three times the sample of mere detection.
B Can the moderation study find its interaction? 4,514 vs. 1,092 4,518 vs. 1,093 The same eight points cost about four times as much as an interaction as they do as a main effect.
C What is last year’s pilot worth? 1,986 vs. 1,819 1,985 vs. 1,822 The pilot contributes its world, never its effect; one changed argument re-prices the design.
D How many firms for a firm-year panel? 572; 699 and 843 573; 701 and 849 Sample size counts firms, rho is the elicitation that matters, and attrition costs firms, not firm-years.
E What does instrumenting the treatment cost? 6,813 vs. 699 6,750 vs. 732 Instrumenting multiplies the requirement almost tenfold; budget for the estimator the analysis will report.

Required sample sizes for 80 percent power, for each design’s own claim: the minimum-effect claim in A, C and D, detection in B and E. A: minimum effect vs. detection. B: the AIE vs. the same effect as a main effect. C: the pilot’s baseline vs. a baseline of 0.25. D: firms in the balanced panel, then with retention of 0.85 and 0.70. E: the control function vs. an exogenous treatment. Each is a seeded estimate accepted by the confirmation run; other seeds move it by a few percent without changing any comparison above.

What to report

A design paragraph in a proposal or a preregistration should let a reader re-run the analysis and judge its assumptions. It reports:

  • the estimand and its units: the APE or the AIE, in probability points, with the model and link;
  • the SESOI, with its substantive justification;
  • the claim, its error rate and the interval level it implies, and how the error rate was chosen;
  • the planning value, the effect at which power was computed, and why;
  • the assumed world and its source: baseline rate, covariates and their dependence, nuisance signal, panel or first-stage quantities where they apply; parametric guesses, pilot rows or a pilot model;
  • that the target is feasible in that world;
  • power at the chosen n with its Monte Carlo standard error, and the full outcome table;
  • the robustness range: what was swept, the range of power and the worst case, and n_max where relevant;
  • the software and its version, the seed and the number of replications.

power_statement() (in Stata, powerape statement) writes the estimand, world, claim and power items as a paragraph; the feasibility check, the robustness range and the seeds come from the same session. For Design A at its required n:

sA <- ape_power(dA, n = nA_min$n, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                nsim = 4000, seed = 20260821)
power_statement(sA)
#> We conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the average partial effect
#> (APE) of program using the powerape package (version 1.11.4), following the
#> confidence-interval approach of Riesthuis (2024). The assumed data-generating
#> process was a probit model with focal variable program (binary, prevalence
#> 0.50); parametric covariates z (continuous, mean 0, SD 1), with the focal
#> variable and the covariates mutually independent; baseline outcome rate 0.300
#> with the focal at reference; nuisance covariates contribute a latent
#> pseudo-R-squared of 0.10. The assumed true APE was 0.100 (10.0 percentage
#> points). At a sample size of n = 2091, simulated power for the minimum-effect
#> claim (the 90% confidence interval's lower bound exceeding the smallest
#> effect size of interest, 0.050; a one-sided test at alpha = 5%) was 0.804
#> (Monte Carlo SE 0.006; 4000 replications). Across replications, the
#> probability of concluding a meaningful effect was 0.804, of detection without
#> meaningfulness 0.194, of an inconclusive result 0.001, and of equivalence
#> 0.000. Estimation used maximum likelihood with delta-method Wald confidence
#> intervals; replications without a maximum-likelihood estimate, from a failed
#> fit or from separation (a focal cell with no events or no non-events),
#> counted against the claim (0.0% of replications).
powerape power a, n(`n_min') claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(4000)         ///
    seed(20260821)

powerape statement
We conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the average partial effect
(APE) of program using the powerape package for Stata (version 0.1.3 (Stata
port of powerape 1.11.3)), following the confidence-interval approach of
Riesthuis (2024). The assumed data-generating process was a probit model with
focal variable program (binary, prevalence 0.50); parametric covariates z
(continuous, mean 0, SD 1), with the focal variable and the covariates
mutually independent; baseline outcome rate 0.300 with the focal at reference;
nuisance covariates contribute a latent pseudo-R-squared of 0.10. The assumed
true APE was 0.100 (10.0 percentage points). At a sample size of n = 2084,
simulated power for the minimum-effect claim (the 90% confidence interval's
lower bound exceeding the smallest effect size of interest, 0.050; a one-sided
test at alpha = 5%) was 0.806 (Monte Carlo SE 0.006; 4000 replications).
Across replications, the probability of concluding a meaningful effect was
0.806, of detection without meaningfulness 0.193, of an inconclusive result
0.002, and of equivalence 0.000. Estimation used maximum likelihood with
delta-method Wald confidence intervals; replications without a
maximum-likelihood estimate, from a failed fit or from separation (a focal
cell with no events or no non-events), counted against the claim (0.0% of
replications).

Notes on reproducibility

  • The R output on this page comes from powerape 1.11.4, the Stata output from the Stata command 0.1.3 (StataNow 19.5). Every call shows its seed and its number of replications, so with the same versions the R numbers reproduce exactly.
  • R and Stata draw different random numbers, so their numbers agree up to simulation error, not digit for digit.
  • A required sample size is confirmed by a run with four times the search’s replications (16,000 in Design E’s instrumented search), and the search never trims n after an overshoot. A required n therefore inherits the noise of the power estimates near the target, and the two languages can land a few percent apart: for Design E’s exogenous comparison, R stops at 699 and Stata at 732, where its confirmation run found a power of .82.
  • In Stata, the single power calls fit every simulated study with Stata’s own commands: probit (with vce(cluster) on the panel route) and cfprobit on the IV route. That is slower: the 4,000 simulated panels of Design D’s first power call took 5 minutes this way, on a machine that was busy with other jobs. The searches and sweeps use the Mata engine, which follows the R package’s conventions and is 10 to 30 times faster; the two engines agree up to simulation error (see How powerape is validated).
  • The Stata code uses the R code’s numbers of replications throughout, except in Design D’s single power calls: 4,000 and 2,000 replications where R uses 20,000 and 10,000: under probit each simulated panel costs Stata many times what it costs R’s engine, so the Stata run keeps these counts down.
  • The Stata runs behind this page are in the package’s repository, in precompute/stata (worked-example-a.do to worked-example-e.do).

References

Wooldridge, J. M. (2015). Control function methods in applied econometrics. Journal of Human Resources, 50(2), 420–445. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.50.2.420
